demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
She first came to my office on a humid Tuesday afternoon, still wearing her olive-green ranger uniform under a lightweight jacket. She sat at the edge of the chair, hands clasped tight in her lap, scanning the room once, twice, before letting her eyes settle on the floor. Her name is Amara, and she is thirty-three years old, an African woman who works as a park ranger in a large national reserve. She has been married for six years. Her PCL-5 score was 46.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago. Amara and her younger brother, Kofi, were both rangers. They had grown up in the shadow of the park, their father a retired ranger, their mother a schoolteacher. Kofi was twenty-nine, quiet, good with animals, always the one who could read the wind. He and Amara often patrolled together. On that day, they responded to a report of poachers near the eastern boundary. It was late afternoon, the light going amber through the acacias. They found the carcass of a rhino, horns roughly hacked off. Then the gunfire came from the thicket. Amara remembers diving behind a termite mound, shouting for Kofi to take cover. He didn't. A single bullet caught him in the throat. She crawled to him, held him as the blood soaked through her shirt, tried to stop it with her hands. The poachers fled. By the time backup arrived, he was gone.

She did not cry at the funeral. She remembers standing in the cemetery, the red earth fresh and heavy, her mother weeping. She felt nothing except a pressure behind her eyes and a numb, electric hum in her skull. That night, she did not sleep. She lay awake, replaying the sound of the shot, the way his body went slack. Over the following weeks, the images became more vivid. She started seeing Kofi in crowds, in the reflection of windows, in the shadow of a tree at dusk. Once, while driving a park vehicle, she slammed on the brakes because she thought she saw him standing on the road. It was a goat.

She stopped going on patrol. She told her supervisor she needed desk duty for a while, citing fatigue. That "while" has stretched into over a year. She now works in the administrative office, processing permits and filing reports. Every time a helicopter flies overhead—the park uses them for anti-poaching surveillance—her heart hammers so hard she feels it in her throat. She avoids the eastern sector entirely, taking a longer route even when it costs her an hour. Loud noises make her flinch. The crack of a branch during a nature walk with her husband, Daniel, sends her into a cold sweat. Daniel has learned not to surprise her from behind. He treads carefully around her, and she hates that.

Her sleep is broken. She has nightmares two or three times a week—Kofi’s face, the blood, the silence after the gunshot. Sometimes she wakes up hitting the mattress, her fists tight, screaming his name. Most nights she lies awake, hyper-aware of every creak in the house, every rustle outside. She has started drinking gin before bed, just enough to dull the edges, but it doesn’t stop the dreams.

At work, she is irritable with colleagues who joke too loudly. She cannot stand the sound of laughter in the break room; it feels like a betrayal. She has withdrawn from her closest friends at the park, people she once camped and hiked with. She tells herself they don't understand, that they would look at her differently if they knew she froze instead of saving him. She believes, in some wordless part of herself, that she should have died instead of Kofi. That her mother lost the wrong child.

She does not talk about Kofi. When her husband brings up his name, she changes the subject or leaves the room. She has not visited his grave since the burial. She avoids looking at photos on her phone. The only thing she keeps is his old ranger hat, which she hung behind the door of her study, out of sight, but she knows it is there.

She told me all this slowly, over several sessions, her voice flat, her hands seldom still. She is a woman holding a trembling engine inside a calm exterior. She does not yet believe that talking can help, but she came because Daniel asked her to, and she came because she is tired of feeling like a stranger to herself.
